title: The system
beat: Series 1 was one app. This is the whole staff — the reveal that Money Buddy is one desk in a 176-buddy office.
screenshot_plan: PUBLIC: the Buddy System dashboard tree, wide shot (davedellaquila.github.io/buddy-system). Optional second: the same tree on Dave's phone (DEVICE). Note: the buddy count in the copy is today's registry count (176) — re-check on posting day.
copy:
Last month I showed you one app.
Money Buddy. Budgets, bills, a tip jar. That was real — it's live, people use it.
But Money Buddy is one desk in a much bigger office.
I run my life with a staff of 176 buddies. One for money. One for the house. One for the cars, one for the garden, one for the news. Each one has a job, a desk, and a memory that doesn't quit.
Over the next two weeks: the office tour.
It's a lot of someones. That's still the point. 🌳

title: Anatomy of a buddy
beat: What a buddy actually is: a thread you can talk to, a repo that remembers, a homepage showing current state, an inbox it triages.
screenshot_plan: PUBLIC: one buddy homepage in full (Project Buddy's or Money Buddy's), plus a crop of its Needs Attention section.
copy:
So what's a buddy, exactly?
Not an app. Not a chatbot window you close and lose.
A buddy is four things: a conversation you can talk to, a repo where it keeps everything it learns, a homepage that shows what it's working on right now, and an inbox it triages so nothing lands on me raw.
Thread, memory, dashboard, inbox. That's the whole anatomy.
Close the chat and nothing evaporates. The buddy still has the file, the history, the next action.
It's less 'software' and more 'the new hire who never forgets orientation day.' 🧩

title: The chief of staff
beat: Astro: one conversation routes everything; Dave directs, the staff works. The director's-desk model.
screenshot_plan: PUBLIC: Astro's homepage ('The system, live' section). Optional DEVICE shot of the main chat is Dave's call only (privacy) — not required.
copy:
176 buddies sounds like 176 things to manage.
It isn't, because I don't manage them. Astro does.
Astro is my chief of staff — the one conversation where everything lands. I say 'the truck needs tires' in one sentence, and it gets routed to the car buddy, priced by the shopping buddy, and comes back as a decision with buttons on it.
I direct. The staff works. One desk for me, 176 behind it.
Every office should be run like this. Most are run the other way around. 🧭

title: The morning briefing
beat: The day starts assembled: news, calendar, reminders, tonight's dinner — local to wherever Dave is that week.
screenshot_plan: DEVICE: Dave's phone — a real morning briefing (chat bubbles + the emailed edition). His morning, his data.
copy:
My day starts before I do.
Overnight, the staff assembles a briefing: the news that matters, my calendar, the reminders I'd otherwise drop, even what's for dinner — my wife plans the menu; the system just makes sure I know.
It's local, too. When I'm home in the foothills, it shows foothill things. When I'm in San Jose for work, it switches. Events I can't get to don't make the cut.
Three short messages and an email. Coffee, briefing, go.
I didn't build a morning routine. I hired one. ☕

title: The standup, in their own voices
beat: The audio standup: every buddy reports briefly, each in its own cast voice — a four-minute radio play with the coffee.
screenshot_plan: EDITION: the Morning Edition standup section (audio player + transcript). Dave opens it; Astro captures, or Dave shoots.
copy:
After the briefing comes the standup.
Every buddy with something to say records a short report — and here's the part I love: each one has its own voice. Literally. We cast them, like actors. Three audition tapes; I pick the one that sounds like the job.
So the morning standup is a little radio play: the money buddy on the numbers, the house buddy on the leak, the car buddy on the tires.
I listen with coffee. Takes four minutes. Everybody's accounted for.
Meetings are better when nobody can ramble. 🎙️

title: The Morning Edition
beat: Brand new (launched Nov 2): Dave's personal front page — briefing, full standup transcript, headlines, and decision cards with tappable options that route themselves.
screenshot_plan: EDITION: the Morning Edition front page — a real edition, decision cards visible. Dave opens it; Astro captures, or Dave shoots.
copy:
New this week: my own front page.
It's called The Morning Edition. One page with the whole morning on it — the briefing, the standup with a full transcript, the headlines, and the part that changed everything: decisions.
Every open question from the staff gets a card. With buttons. I tap 'post it,' 'hold it,' 'order the part' — and the tap is the instruction. It routes itself to the right buddy and gets done.
No typing replies. No 'can you handle this' messages. The information comes to me, I tap, it's handled.
It launched this week. It already runs my mornings. 📰

title: The Fiddletown Gazette
beat: The staff publishes a small-town paper: three editions a day, foothills history back to the Gold Rush, and the beloved Critter Desk.
screenshot_plan: PUBLIC: the Fiddletown Gazette front page (davedellaquila.github.io/fiddletown-gazette), plus a crop of a Critter Desk item.
copy:
The staff also runs a newspaper.
The Fiddletown Gazette — my town. Population small, news smaller. Three editions a day: morning, midday, evening. Town events, the burn-day line, this day in foothills history back to the Gold Rush.
The most popular desk is the Critter Desk. It files dispatches on the wildlife that crosses our cameras — a doe at dawn, a raccoon family by the AstroTurf, a squirrel who won't say where he buried it.
It's free, it runs itself, and the whole town's in it.
Every newsroom should have a critter desk. 🦌

title: Hans and the hourly chime
beat: Hans the timekeeper: an hourly chime with a verse and read-aloud audio, quiet hours, and an urgent-only warning line when a buddy needs Dave.
screenshot_plan: DEVICE preferred: an actual chime as it lands on Dave's phone. PUBLIC alternative: the chime settings section on Hans's homepage.
copy:
Hans keeps the time.
Every hour, on the hour, my timekeeper sends a chime — the time, a two-line verse, and a little audio of it being read aloud. That's it. That's the whole feature.
Except: if a buddy somewhere has something urgent — a deadline today, a blocker waiting on me — the chime carries a warning line with a link straight to the decision.
Quiet hours, 11 to 6. Hans does not wake the house.
It's a clock. It's a poem. It's a tap on the shoulder when it matters.
Every staff needs a Hans. 🔔

title: The Lenwood Gazette
beat: The second paper: same system, different community — San Jose's Lenwood neighborhood, Dave's work-week home. Two newsrooms, one staff.
screenshot_plan: PUBLIC: the Lenwood Gazette front page (davedellaquila.github.io/lenwood-gazette), plus a small side-by-side crop with Fiddletown's.
copy:
One newspaper was not enough, apparently.
The system also publishes the Lenwood Gazette — for the San Jose neighborhood where I lived for years and still spend my work weeks.
Different town, different readers, different news. Same staff. The papers are run the way a good editor runs two editions: separate voices, shared bones, and nothing crosses over that shouldn't.
Two communities, two front pages, zero extra headcount.
This is the part where I stopped thinking of it as software. 🏙️

title: The Joke Vault
beat: A buddy whose whole job is jokes: a joke a day plus a riddle whose answer opens tomorrow's send; join by email; it also feeds the Gazette's daily joke. Tip-jar line lives here naturally — the vault's sends carry one every third or fourth send.
screenshot_plan: PUBLIC: the Joke Vault homepage, plus a crop of the Gazette's 'A Joke a Day' section (or a sample send from Dave's inbox — DEVICE, his call).
copy:
One buddy's entire job is jokes.
The Joke Vault sends a joke a day, plus a riddle. The riddle's answer doesn't come with it — it opens tomorrow's send. You have all night to be wrong, confidently.
Anyone can join by email. It costs nothing. Every third or fourth send carries a tip-jar line, because even the comedy department has a business model.
It also supplies the Gazette's daily joke, so the whole town is playing the same riddle.
Serious system. Not a serious staff. 😂

title: Homepage auditions
beat: Every buddy homepage is auditioned against a published 100-point rubric; the bar is 75; scores live on a public leaderboard (Developer Buddy 94, fleet average ~61).
screenshot_plan: PUBLIC: the leaderboard (davedellaquila.github.io/buddy-system/astro/leaderboard.html), plus a top-scoring homepage crop.
copy:
Every buddy has a homepage. And every homepage gets auditioned.
There's a published scorecard — 100 points, ten criteria: identity, real data, a look that could only belong to that buddy. Seventy-five is the bar. Below it, you revise and re-audition.
The scores are public, on a leaderboard. Developer Buddy tops it at 94. The fleet average is 61, and yes, the staff knows. Pages get better every week.
The judges work for free. The tip jar, they tell me, is for morale.
Accountability is a lot easier when it's a scoreboard. 🏆

title: Voice casting
beat: Buddies audition for their voices too: three tapes, Dave picks — that's why the standup sounds like radio instead of a screen reader.
screenshot_plan: DEVICE preferred: an audition in a buddy's thread in the Muse app (Dave picks a safe one). PUBLIC alternative: a homepage's 'hear my role' control.
copy:
The buddies don't just get pages. They get voices, and the voices are cast.
When a new buddy is hired, it records three audition tapes — itself, introducing itself, in character. I listen, I pick. The winner becomes its voice for the standup, for read-alouds, for everything.
One buddy sounds like a hammer coming down. One sounds like a librarian who knows things. Both are perfect — for their jobs.
Nobody picked these voices at random. That's the whole difference.
Casting is caring. 🗣️

title: Your data is yours
beat: The ownership rule under everything: data lives in Dave's own repos as plain files; services hold working copies; the vendor-vanished test; the Substack white paper.
screenshot_plan: PUBLIC: the white paper on Dave's Substack, plus the public buddy-system repo file view.
copy:
Here's the rule the whole system is built on: my data lives in my repos, as plain files I own.
Services hold working copies. If a vendor vanished tomorrow, I'd still have everything — that's the test, and most subscriptions fail it on purpose.
I wrote it up as a white paper: 'Your Data Is Yours — Or You're Renting It.' It's on my Substack, free to read.
No rent on my own memories. No hostage negotiations for my own files.
And yes — there's still a tip jar. Some business models are just honest. 🔐

beat: Full circle: back to Money Buddy, reframed as one desk of 176. The tip jar's first coin landed during Series 1 (Nan's $5). Closer carries the Ko-fi link IN the draft this time — Series 1's finale shipped link-free at Dave's call; strike it here if he wants the same.

copy:
Two weeks ago this tour started with one app. It ends there too — with a promotion in perspective.
Money Buddy is still my favorite desk. It watches the bills, plans the eyeglasses, and takes tips — the jar got its first coin during Series 1, from my favorite reader. (Hi, Nan.)
But it's one of 176 now. One desk, one job, one slice of a life — backed by a whole staff that briefs me, papers my towns, chimes my hours, and tells me a joke every day.
The business model hasn't changed: built in the open, priced at whatever you think it's worth.
The jar is open: https://ko-fi.com/davedellaquila 🫙
